raw_case_text:
A 34-year-old Cypriot male, with unremarkable past medical history, was admitted for investigation after complaining for blunt diffuse abdominal pain, starting a month ago, without any other constitutional symptoms. He denied the use of any recreational drugs or alcohol, recent traveling abroad or contact with any pets.
The physical examination was unremarkable. However, a right upper quadrant abdominal tenderness during deep palpation and a positive Murphy sign were present. The patient had also poor oral hygiene.
Laboratory examination was normal, besides a mild hypochromic microcytic anemia and a mild C-reaction protein (CRP) elevation (WBCs: 9.570/mul, neutrophils %: 67%, hemoglobin: 10.0 g/dl, mean corpuscular volume 75.9 fl, mean corpuscular hemoglobin: 23.4 fl and CRP 54.47 mg/l).
Abdominal ultrasonography showed a sizable liver lesion (cyst containing) confirmed by abdominal computed tomography (CT) scan (Fig. 1a). Patient was initiated intravenous metronidazole 500 mg three times daily and piperacillin/tazobactam 4.5 g three times daily. Blood and stool cultures were negative. Further investigation with procalcitonin, tuberculin skin test, serology for Echinococcus granulosus and hepatitis/HIV screening was negative. The abscess was drained under CT guidance and the fluid's biochemistry examination (Fig. 1c) was compatible with exudative etiology (pus; WBCs: 83.600/mul, neutrophils (#): 48 400, glucose 0 mg/dl, protein: 5.49 g/dl and LDH fluid/serum ratio: 8.16). Fluid's cytologic examination was negative and the gram stain showed necrotic WBCs. Streptococcus intermedius and M. luteus/lylae sensitive to oral beta-lactams were isolated from the fluid culture. 
Transthoracic echocardiograph excluded infectious endocarditis. Endoscopic evaluation of the gastrointestinal tract revealed only internal hemorrhoids. Dentist referral concluded to a poor oral hygiene and an increased plaque deposition (Fig. 1d).
Follow-up with an ultrasound a day before removing the drainage catheter showed a residual abscess cavity (dimensions of 5.3 x 1.4 cm) with minimal effusion and air (Fig. 1b). The drainage catheter was removed after a week. After 23 days, the patient was discharged after switching to oral antimicrobial therapy, deescalating to amoxicillin/clavulanic acid 625 mg and metronidazole 400 mg three times daily, respectively, to complete 6 weeks of antibiotic therapy. Furthermore, the patient was scheduled for complete dental care, to ensure that poor oral hygiene will not be an infection source once again.
However, a week after his discharge, the patient was admitted to the General Surgery Department with high fever, shivering, abdominal pain, generalized maculopapular rash and diarrhea. From laboratory evaluation, the patient did not present leukocytosis (WBCs: 6.090/mul); however, other inflammation markers were elevated (CRP: 147.8 mg/l). Ultrasonography and abdominal CT imaging revealed a relapse of the abscess and the patient undergone a surgical abscess drainage, in combination with broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotic therapy with successful outcome. Cultures of pus after surgical drainage were positive for S. intermedius.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 34-year-old Cypriot male presented with a 1-month history of dull diffuse abdominal pain.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient experienced blunt, diffuse abdominal pain for 1 month without fever or other constitutional symptoms.
subjective.past_medical_history: Unremarkable past medical history; denied alcohol or recreational drug use, recent travel abroad, or contact with pets.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for diffuse abdominal pain; negative for constitutional symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Right upper quadrant tenderness on deep palpation with a positive Murphy's sign, and poor oral hygiene with heavy dental plaque deposition; otherwise unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: Labs showed mild hypochromic microcytic anemia (hemoglobin 10.0 g/dL, MCV 75.9 fL, MCH 23.4 pg), WBC 9,570/uL (67% neutrophils), elevated CRP (54.47 mg/L), normal procalcitonin, and negative blood/stool cultures, tuberculin skin test, Echinococcus granulosus serology, and hepatitis/HIV screens. Transthoracic echocardiography was normal. Abdominal ultrasound revealed a large cyst-containing hepatic lesion.
objective.advanced_workup: Abdominal CT confirmed a large hepatic abscess. CT-guided percutaneous drainage yielded purulent exudate (WBC 83,600/uL, neutrophils 48,400/uL, glucose 0 mg/dL, protein 5.49 g/dL, fluid/serum LDH ratio 8.16, negative cytology) that grew beta-lactam-susceptible Streptococcus intermedius and Micrococcus luteus/lylae. Upper/lower GI endoscopy showed only internal hemorrhoids. When the abscess relapsed 1 week post-discharge with high fever, rigors, maculopapular rash, diarrhea, and CRP 147.8 mg/L (WBC 6,090/uL), repeat CT and open surgical drainage again cultured Streptococcus intermedius.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Pyogenic liver abscess caused by Streptococcus intermedius and Micrococcus luteus/lylae secondary to severe periodontal disease/poor oral hygiene (hepatic hydatid cyst excluded by negative Echinococcus granulosus serology and purulent bacterial culture). Initial CT-guided percutaneous drainage and IV piperacillin/tazobactam (4.5 g TID) plus metronidazole (500 mg TID) followed by oral amoxicillin/clavulanate and metronidazole was complicated by abscess relapse 1 week post-discharge, which was curatively treated with open surgical drainage, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, and comprehensive dental care.
